Hold affected event keys using the existing queue or quarantine procedure. Add a seeded orphan-with-pending-retry test that proves no second order or success acknowledgment occurs while held. Reconcile only from trusted immutable event identity, canonical payload, and committed-order evidence; keep missing or conflicting evidence quarantined for owner review. Do not invent fingerprints, delete receipts, or replay an unresolved legacy event.

Use only the supplied packet and repository unless I identify another approved source. Access only the explicitly approved read-only monitoring source, if supplied. Write code and task artifacts only in this repository; use only its isolated test database. Do not connect directly to production application or database hosts, or modify production systems. Do not replay production events, modify live data or monitoring, create or post external updates, merge, or deploy. 

Give Codex one bounded incident to investigate in a prepared cloud environment. The goal is a result an engineer can review: a supported explanation, a regression test that fails before the fix, a focused patch, and evidence from the tests that ran.

This works well after the immediate incident has been stabilized and the remaining job is to understand and fix an application defect. If the available evidence cannot establish the cause, a useful result is a clear account of the investigation and the next diagnostic step.

Prepare the environment and incident packet

In the web or desktop app, choose Work in > Cloud and select a published environment.

To create one, select Create environment, choose the GitHub repositories, and ask Codex to prepare the runtime, dependencies, and isolated test services.

Review the setup report, resolve failed checks, and Publish before starting a new task.

Follow the current Cloud environment guide.

Keep repository guidance in AGENTS.md.

If dependencies change or service setup changes, edit the reusable environment, test it, and Republish; then validate the updated environment in a new task.

Repository refresh does not rerun install/start commands, and existing tasks retain their own state.

Configure required network destinations and test credentials separately; allowing a destination does not grant service access.

Confirm that the affected checkout, dependencies, checks, and disposable test database work in the new task. Record the starting commit and test baseline.

Keep the initial investigation self-contained. Place a sanitized packet in the repository or make its files available to the task. An engineer should assemble and check it before starting:

Input
What to include

Incident summary
Incident ID, UTC time window, expected and observed behavior, known impact, and current status. Distinguish confirmed counts from estimates.

Release identity
The deployed commit SHA, deployment time, relevant configuration values without secrets, and the last known good release if available.

Correlated evidence
Log and trace excerpts with timestamps, event IDs, request IDs, trace IDs, and file references. Preserve identifiers consistently when sanitizing.

Safe reproduction
Test request bodies, relevant fixtures, and instructions for exercising the suspected path without calling live services.

Repository guidance
Relevant paths, database engine, test commands, permitted changes, and the engineer who will review the result.

Do not include access tokens, customer payloads, or personal data in the packet.

A monitoring integration is optional. If you use one, grant read-only access to the relevant project and time window; the file-based workflow does not require it. Repository instructions should keep test credentials separate from production configuration.

Run the starter prompt

Use the starter prompt on this page and replace its placeholders with your incident ID, repository, and packet path. The first result should connect the evidence to the affected code, explain what can be reproduced, and identify missing information.

Ask Codex to continue through implementation only when the evidence supports a code defect. Otherwise, review the investigation and provide the missing input. A plausible explanation, a recent code change, or a successful test on a different release is not enough to establish the cause.

Example: A retried webhook creates a duplicate order

Use the runnable incident sample to practice the investigation. It includes a prepared incident packet, a handler with a reproducible defect, the corrected handler, and PostgreSQL tests.

The service receives an order.created webhook, writes an order, and records that the event has been processed. During an incident, a retry appears to create a second order. The team has already stabilized the service and wants a patch for review.

The sample uses JavaScript, Node.js’s test runner, and PostgreSQL. Its disposable fixture has an event_receipts table with non-null identity columns and a non-deferrable unique key on (provider, account_id, event_id).

The schema permits a receipt claim before the order exists and retains the canonical payload fingerprint needed to detect conflicting reuse of the same event key.

If your application instead requires an order foreign key at claim time or lacks this conflict evidence, stop for a separate schema/design decision.

Record the exact runtime, dependency lock, PostgreSQL version, transaction isolation level, and receipt schema in the evidence. The downloadable fixture pins Node.js 24.19.0, PostgreSQL 17.6, and pg 8.23.1.

For the supplied Compose setup, prepare an environment with a working Docker daemon and verify docker info before publishing it. Its database accepts only public test credentials and is bound to the local loopback interface. Use your application’s database engine and relevant settings when adapting the test.

This example assumes PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, stable provider event IDs, and receipt retention covering the provider’s retry/replay window.

The fixed handler places receipt and order writes in one database transaction. The fixture provisions a disposable database and a delivery_holds table to model an existing queue’s quarantine procedure; that table is test infrastructure, not a proposed application migration.

The application fix adds no queue, database service, schema migration, or monitoring integration. If those assumptions do not hold, stop and revise the scope.

Run the sample

Extract the ZIP, open its directory, and use Docker with Compose:

docker compose -p codex-incident-rehearsal up -d --wait postgres
docker compose -p codex-incident-rehearsal run --rm runner node main.mjs baseline
docker compose -p codex-incident-rehearsal run --rm runner node main.mjs regression
docker compose -p codex-incident-rehearsal run --rm runner
docker compose -p codex-incident-rehearsal down --volumes

The baseline command must exit with code 1: the retry assertion observes two orders and one receipt instead of one of each. The regression command runs the same assertion against the corrected handler and must exit with code 0.

The final test command exercises the full matrix, including independent connections, database lock contention, and legacy-orphan quarantine.

If your installation provides docker-compose, use that spelling in place of docker compose. Run these commands sequentially; the suite resets only its marked test schema.

Inspect the transaction handler

This excerpt comes from main.mjs in the download. Run the complete files after extracting the ZIP; the tests and fixture setup are included there.

Receipt claim and order transaction
async function fixed(client, input, hook = async (_boundary) => {}) {
await assertNotHeld(client, input);
await hook("beforeClaim");
await client.query("BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED");
let committed = false;
try {
const claimed = await client.query(
`INSERT INTO event_receipts(provider, account_id, event_id, payload_fingerprint)
VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4)
ON CONFLICT (provider, account_id, event_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING event_id`,
[...key(input), fingerprint(input)]
);
trace("receipt-claim-result", client, input, {
inserted: claimed.rowCount === 1,
});
if (claimed.rowCount === 1) {
await hook("afterClaim");
await writeOrder(client, input);
await hook("afterOrder");
} else {
// A new READ COMMITTED statement sees the winner after its commit.
await checkReceipt(client, input);
}
await client.query("COMMIT");
committed = true;
trace("transaction-committed", client, input);
await hook("afterCommit");
trace("acknowledged", client, input, acknowledgment);
return acknowledgment;
} catch (error) {
if (!committed) {
await client.query("ROLLBACK");
trace("transaction-rolled-back-no-ack", client, input);
} else {
trace("committed-response-lost-no-ack", client, input);
}
throw error;
}
}

1. Provide a compact packet

Use these files as the packet outline:

incidents/INC-DEMO-014/incident.md
incidents/INC-DEMO-014/logs.ndjson
incidents/INC-DEMO-014/release.json
incidents/INC-DEMO-014/order-created.sanitized.json

In this scenario, release.json identifies the example release SHA 4a1c9e7d2b6f8a0c3d5e7f9012a4b6c8d0e2f413, deployed at 2026-09-22T11:58:00Z. The incident window is 12:03:00Z–12:05:00Z on the same day. The packet reports two internal orders associated with one provider event. When preparing your own packet, include confirmed impact counts and identify any estimates.

The sanitized logs contain these correlated observations:

UTC time
Correlation
Observation

12:03:04.110
Event evt_demo_042, account acct_demo_01, request req_demo_a, trace trace_demo_a
First delivery enters the webhook handler.

12:03:04.145
Same event and first trace
Order ord_demo_101 is committed.

12:03:04.150
Same worker
Worker exits before a receipt-write success or response is recorded. The excerpt alone does not prove the receipt is absent.

12:03:14.203
Same provider/account/event, request req_demo_b, trace trace_demo_b
A retry enters the handler. The handler logs that no matching receipt was found.

12:03:14.241
Same event and second trace
Order ord_demo_102 is committed and a receipt is recorded.

Keep a stable event ID across deliveries and distinct request and trace IDs per delivery. A per-request identifier would hide the relationship between the retry and the original event.

2. Trace the evidence and test the hypothesis

The incident report proposes that a retry storm caused the duplicate. Codex should treat that as a hypothesis. Two observed deliveries do not establish a storm, and retries are a normal condition a webhook handler must tolerate.

In the sample’s affected implementation, source inspection reveals this sequence: look up a receipt, commit the order, then write the receipt in a separate transaction. The gap between the two commits is a stronger explanation. A worker failure in that gap can leave an order without a receipt, so a retry can create another order. Concurrent deliveries can also both pass a separate check before either writes its receipt.

Have Codex trace the actual handler and transaction boundaries and cite the relevant lines. It should confirm the packet’s release matches the code under test, or explain why testing a different commit limits the conclusion.

3. Reproduce before changing the handler

Add a regression test using the sample webhook and the isolated PostgreSQL database. Put a test-only failure hook immediately after the order write and before the receipt-write step in the original handler.

Confirm from the real transaction boundaries that the original order has committed at that point. Retry the same provider/account/event and assert exactly one order and one matching receipt; the seeded implementation should fail with two orders.

After the fix, exercise the corresponding hook after the order statement but before the shared transaction commits; the failed attempt must leave zero orders and zero receipts.

Retry and assert one of each. Keep the same business assertion across revisions and record the hook location on each revision.

Run the new test on the original implementation first. For the seeded defect in this sample, the expected failure is two orders instead of one. Save the command, starting commit, exit code, and assertion output. If that failure does not occur, investigate the mismatch before editing the handler.

An injected exception exercises the application’s transaction behavior. Record that it does not reproduce every possible host, network, or database failure.

4. Make the smallest supported fix

For this specific defect, claim the event receipt and write the order within one transaction on one database connection. Use the existing unique key with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (provider, account_id, event_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING ....

Only the delivery that inserts the receipt may write the order; acknowledge success only after commit. A failed transaction rolls back both writes. Do not catch a uniqueness error and continue using an aborted transaction.

A competing delivery may wait for the first transaction. If the first commits, the second claim inserts nothing: issue a fresh SELECT under READ COMMITTED, verify the stored event identity/payload policy, and return the existing duplicate acknowledgment without writing an order.

If the first transaction rolls back, the competitor can claim and process the event. A missing receipt after a skipped insert, an identity conflict, or a transient database error must follow the documented retry/error path, not a fabricated success.

Under stricter isolation, serialization failures require the repository’s bounded whole-transaction retry policy. See PostgreSQL’s INSERT conflict behavior and transaction isolation.

Neither an in-memory set nor a separate “check then insert” protects against concurrent workers or restarts. Scope the key to the provider’s event-identity contract. If a supposedly identical event carries conflicting identity or payload information, surface that inconsistency rather than silently treating it as a valid duplicate.

The demo’s business mutation is entirely within the same database. If the real handler also sends email, charges a card, or calls another service, this transaction alone does not make those external effects idempotent. Identify that boundary and the system’s existing delivery or idempotency mechanism before expanding the fix.

5. Verify the changed behavior

Ask for both the original failure and the post-fix result. Use test-only hooks at named transaction boundaries and inspect committed state from a separate connection. The sample passes eleven local PostgreSQL tests; test-evidence.md in the download records those results and the checks still needed for Cloud execution and deployment. Run the suite in your published environment and test actual connection loss during commit before relying on that recovery path.

Check / failure point
Required behavior

First delivery and committed duplicate
The first creates one order and one receipt; a repeated event returns the agreed acknowledgment and leaves counts unchanged. Record exact status/body.

Before receipt claim
Failure creates neither row and returns no success acknowledgment. A retry creates one of each.

After claim, before order write
Failure rolls back the receipt; no order exists. A retry can claim and process normally.

After order write, before commit
Failure rolls back both rows. This is the fixed-code counterpart of the original committed-order/missing-receipt defect; a retry leaves one of each.

After commit, before acknowledgment
Simulate a lost response. Both rows remain committed. A retry returns the duplicate acknowledgment without another order.

Commit outcome unknown
Model a connection loss around commit separately from an ordinary exception. Return no unsupported success claim; a retry with the same stable event key must be safe whether the first transaction committed or rolled back. If this transport case was not exercised, mark it not run.

Concurrent duplicate: first transaction commits
Two independent connections/workers contend on the same event key. Hold the winner after claim; start the competitor before releasing it. Verify the competitor actually contends, then release the winner. Both complete through the expected acknowledgment path; exactly one order and one receipt exist.

Concurrent duplicate: first transaction rolls back
Repeat the controlled overlap, but fail the claimant before commit. The competitor claims after rollback and creates one order and one receipt. Check both responses and final state.

Event identity and payload conflict
Different events and the same event ID under different accounts/providers remain independent. For an event with the same scoped ID but a conflicting canonical payload, follow the agreed conflict path; do not create a second order or silently acknowledge different work.

Legacy order without receipt and pending retry
Seed a committed legacy order without a receipt. Identify and hold its event key before retries resume. A held retry returns no success acknowledgment and creates no row. Trusted reconciliation permits the duplicate acknowledgment with one existing order and one receipt; missing or conflicting evidence keeps the key held.

Broader service checks
Run relevant integration tests, lint, and type checking. Separate new failures, pre-existing failures, and checks that could not run.

Coordinate concurrency with barriers/latches and bounded timeouts, not sleeps or a bare pair of promises. Release blocked workers in test cleanup and use disposable fixtures. An exception test alone does not prove abrupt process death, transport loss, or production concurrency behavior.

The sample uses node main.mjs baseline, node main.mjs regression, and node main.mjs inside the pinned runner. Its structured output records transaction boundaries, committed row counts, acknowledgment status/body, and observed blocking backend IDs.

When adapting the workflow, use the commands actually defined by your repository and report their real results. A skipped check or unavailable dependency belongs in the handoff, with its impact on confidence.

Review the handoff

Shared evidence record

Use the incident workflow’s evidence format for each acceptance criterion. Populate it from observed output; the fields below are a template, not passing results. For a new test that does not exist at baseline, distinguish “not yet present” from a failed existing check.

Criterion / test: [specific behavior and test location]
Environment: [published setup reference; runtime, database and dependency versions]
Before: [revision + test-only diff ID; command; exit code; observed assertion; log path]
After: [final revision or base + diff ID; command; exit code; observed assertion; log path]
Status: [pass / fail / blocked / not run]
Limits / reviewer action: [untested behavior, blocker, or decision required]

Keep red and green runs tied to their actual tested states, including test-only changes on the original revision. Keep the logs, response fixtures, and final diff with the handoff. A changed final revision needs updated evidence; checks that were not run or were blocked cannot count as passing.

Ask Codex to leave the code diff and these review artifacts in the repository:

incident-investigation.md: timeline, evidence references, hypotheses tested, supported cause, and remaining uncertainty.

test-evidence.md: baseline commit, failing regression output, fix commit or diff, passing targeted checks, broader checks, and limitations.

pr-draft.md: a concise explanation of the defect, changed behavior, test evidence, and remaining risk.

deployment-handoff.md: verified schema/isolation/receipt-retention assumptions, named rollout owner, pre-deployment checks, duplicate-order and acknowledgment/error metrics, and the rollout/rollback gates below.

Before accepting the patch, verify that the original code fails the new test, the fix passes it, and the diff addresses the demonstrated defect. In the webhook example, inspect event-key scope, transaction boundaries, concurrency coverage, and any effects outside the transaction. Review existing duplicate orders separately; preventing new duplicates does not repair historical records.

Plan deployment and rollback

A code patch protects only workers running the corrected handler. Old workers can still write an order before claiming a receipt, so a mixed-version canary is not evidence that the defect is eliminated.

The deployment owner must choose either a tested mixed-version strategy or an existing runbook that pauses ingestion, drains in-flight old workers, updates every consumer, and resumes retained deliveries without loss.

Confirm the provider/queue retry and retention behavior before choosing the latter; do not assume pausing is lossless.

Before resuming retained deliveries, identify committed legacy orders with no matching receipt. Pausing and draining old consumers prevents new legacy writes; it does not repair those existing orders. Hold every affected event key with the existing queue or quarantine procedure. If legacy records cannot establish a complete event identity, keep the affected deliveries or those from the affected time window paused for owner review rather than declaring the scan complete.

Reconcile a held key only when trusted immutable provider/account/event identity, canonical payload evidence, and the committed business record establish what already happened.

Under the approved reconciliation procedure, record the matching receipt without repeating the business mutation, then release that key’s hold.

Keep affected keys quarantined for owner review when evidence is missing, payloads conflict, or multiple business records exist. A retry payload cannot substitute for trusted evidence of the original event when reconstructing its fingerprint.

The pre-resume gate passes only when each affected key is reconciled or its hold remains enforced across all consumers.

Seed a legacy order and its pending retry in staging. Verify the hold prevents another order and any success acknowledgment; after trusted reconciliation, the retry may receive the duplicate acknowledgment while the existing order count stays at one. Rehearse an unresolved case too: it must remain held without a fabricated receipt. Keep this gate in the deployment handoff alongside pause/drain, consumer-version, retention, and rollback checks.

Before rollout, verify the existing unique constraint is present and valid, the receipt key/payload policy is consistent across all consumers, receipt cleanup cannot reopen the replay window, and external effects remain outside this patch.

In staging, rehearse the selected sequence and failed-worker retry. Record the owner’s observation window and stop thresholds for duplicate orders, webhook errors, acknowledgment latency, lock waits, and retry backlog; do not invent production thresholds.

Reverting to the old handler can reintroduce duplicate orders. The rollback handoff must name the containment step (for example, the approved pause/drain procedure), the safe revision, and the owner who decides when processing can resume. Preserve receipts; do not delete them to unblock retries. Historical duplicate orders require a separately reviewed remediation.

The engineer owns the deployment decision and any production remediation. A passing isolated test is evidence for review, not proof that production is healthy. Create the pull request, run your normal CI and review process, and deploy through your team’s established controls after reviewing the draft.

Continue in the same task

Use a focused follow-up to resolve uncertainty or improve the handoff:

Review the patch against two concurrent deliveries and a retry after a worker failure. Show which behaviors the tests establish and which remain untested. Keep the change limited to this handler and its regression tests; update the handoff with any remaining risk.

If the first run could not reproduce the incident:

Stop implementation. List the hypotheses the evidence rules out, the strongest remaining hypothesis, and the smallest additional sanitized input or isolated experiment needed to distinguish it. Keep the root cause unconfirmed.

Related use cases

Ask Codex to create a composable CLI it can run from any folder, combine with repo scripts...

title: Migrate a validation module
summary: Upgrade one module and prove that its public behavior still holds.

prompts.label: Starter prompt
prompts.text:
Migrate [module] in [repository] from [current pinned version] to [approved target version] in this cloud environment.

Read AGENTS.md, [migration brief], [official migration guide], the dependency lockfile, the module's callers, and [contract test locations]. Record the starting commit, environment/setup reference, installed Python version, framework/Pydantic/bundled-v1 versions, and lockfile hash. Confirm baseline/target compatibility; treat shared dependency/import preparation as a separate reviewed change.

First run [baseline commands], inventory the migration surface, and write a short plan in [plan file]. Preserve [public contracts]. Keep [out-of-scope modules] unchanged. Remove obsolete code only inside the approved slice; name any compatibility adapter that must remain.

If the slice can be isolated and the baseline is usable, run the same frozen HTTP contract tests before and after the change through the real router, error handler, and response serialization. Compare status codes, contractual headers, accepted/rejected inputs, public JSON keys/types, defaults/nulls, and the complete error envelope. Run affected integration, lint and type checks too. If this requires broader upgrades or public behavior changes, return that decision before expanding scope. Do not approve new snapshots, normalize away public differences or weaken assertions. Record each check's revisions/environment/versions, before/after commands, exit codes, evidence paths, and pass/fail/blocked/not run with limitations.

Return the diff, before-and-after evidence, unresolved differences, dependency and lockfile changes, rollback instructions, and a draft PR description. Create a draft PR only if the connected repository tools and my permissions support it; otherwise provide the patch and description. Do not merge, deploy, change production data, or begin another slice.

When to use it

Use this workflow when a migration has a clear boundary and tests that compare old and new behavior. Give Codex a migration brief, the module and its callers, frozen contract fixtures, and a prepared cloud environment. Ask for one focused change with evidence and a rollback path.

The sample migrates one validation model in an orders service from Pydantic v1 to v2. It includes the original implementation, a compatibility preparation stage, and the final module. Its tests exercise the real FastAPI router, error handler, response serialization, adjacent legacy route, and public OpenAPI document. No database migration or deployment is included.

Prepare the cloud environment

Choose Work in > Cloud and select a published environment.

To create one, select Create environment, choose the GitHub repositories, and ask Codex to prepare the runtime, dependencies, and isolated test services.

Review the setup report, resolve failed checks, and Publish before starting a new task.

Follow the Cloud environment guide.

Keep repository guidance in AGENTS.md.

If dependencies change or service setup changes, edit the reusable environment, test it, and Republish.

Validate the updated environment in a new task. Repository refresh preserves dependency caches without rerunning installation or startup commands, and existing tasks retain their own state.

Configure required network destinations and credentials separately.

Record the environment/setup reference, source commit, Python patch version, framework and dependency versions, package-manager version, and lockfile hash at each stage. Verify those versions inside the new task before using its results.

Run the sample

Download the complete migration sample. It includes three standalone uv projects, their resolved uv.lock files, application implementations, a shared error and schema adapter, frozen HTTP fixtures, and the contract runner.

Use Python 3.11, 3.12, or 3.13 and install uv, then run:

unzip sample.zip
cd migrate-a-validation-module
uv run --project support/target --python python3 --frozen python run.py --compare-stages --output evidence

The comparison creates a separate .venv for each stage and installs dependencies with uv sync --frozen. All stages use the invoking Python interpreter and the same HTTP and schema fixtures; dependency versions remain locked.

Python 3.14 and later are excluded because the legacy Pydantic v1 bridge does not support them. A successful run ends with:

PASS: legacy, prepared, target HTTP/schema/serialization contracts match
Native model schemas differ; the existing public schema adapter is preserved.

Read evidence/legacy.json, prepared.json, target.json, and summary.json. They contain observed responses, runtime versions, source, fixture, and lockfile hashes, commands, exit codes, and raw-log paths.

The runner exercises the sample application’s HTTP endpoints through FastAPI’s in-process TestClient. Run it inside your chosen Cloud task and retain that task’s evidence.

Run python3 run.py without --compare-stages only to check the target model in an environment with Pydantic v2 installed. That self-contained mode checks seven validation and serialization cases. It does not run HTTP or cross-stage parity checks. Use the full comparison command above to verify a migration.

The full comparison checks 23 HTTP cases in each stage, public OpenAPI, and response serialization. It passed locally on Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13. The download’s README.md records the tested versions and execution history. Run the current comparison in your Cloud environment to record its results there.

Keep the dependency stages separate

Stage
Python / FastAPI / Pydantic
Migration boundary

Legacy
3.11–3.13 / 0.119.0 / 1.10.22
Existing models import from pydantic.

Prepared baseline
3.11–3.13 / 0.119.0 / 2.12.3
Both models use pydantic.v1. Record the actual bundled-v1 version.

Target
3.11–3.13 / 0.119.0 / 2.12.3
Only OrderInput moves to v2. The adjacent route keeps its separate v1 model.

The prepared and target dependency locks are identical. The module slice changes the model and its direct serialization method, not the dependency environment.

The preparation step is a separate reviewed change. It also makes the remaining v1 route adapters emit alias-keyed dictionaries with dict(by_alias=True) before response validation; returning the v1 model directly under the v2 host can lose public aliases.

The target order adapter uses model_dump(by_alias=True), and the adjacent v1 route keeps its preparation adapter.

The FastAPI migration guide limits temporary mixed v1/v2 route support to 0.119.0 through 0.127.x; 0.128.0 removed it.

This example deliberately pins 0.119.0 to demonstrate that transition. Use a fully v2 boundary for a newer FastAPI application, and keep an owner and removal condition for the temporary bridge. Do not nest v1 and v2 models. This bridge is not a Python 3.14 migration path.

Review the contract tests

The frozen HTTP cases cover successful requests, an omitted note or a note explicitly set to null, missing and invalid IDs, multiple unknown fields, mixed field errors, invalid notes, malformed JSON, wrong content type, missing body, aliases, array and string bodies, and the adjacent legacy route. They compare status codes, the Content-Type header, and complete parsed JSON responses without stripping error fields or changing expected types.

The service has an application-owned error envelope and public OpenAPI document from the legacy stage. The error and schema adapters remain in place. The target preserves the legacy error order: declared-field errors first, then unknown keys alphabetically.

The tests compare the complete ordered error.fields array; they do not sort observed responses. The runner records each model’s native schema separately and verifies that native schemas differ; public schema parity does not mean the dependency’s generated schemas are identical.

The service preserves a legacy input behavior: it accepts an array of pairs such as [["order_id", "ord_123"]] as an object, and both [] and an empty JSON string become empty objects with a missing-ID error. A nonempty string remains an invalid body. The target model keeps successful dict(value) conversions. Changing it to object-only input requires an owner’s contract decision, not a rewritten test expectation.

For your repository, freeze its actual existing responses before editing. Preserve optional fields with explicit defaults, keep strictness and unknown-field behavior, and test the real error handler and response serialization.

Raw validation errors differ across versions. The Pydantic migration guide also describes changes to aliases, coercion, optional fields, and custom validation functions; v2 does not convert TypeError raised inside those functions into ValidationError.

Inspect the contract runner

This excerpt comes from run.py in the download. Run the complete files after extracting the ZIP; the locked stages and HTTP fixtures are included there.

Compare the three stages
class OrderInput(BaseModel):
internal_order_id: StrictStr = Field(alias="order_id")
customer_note: StrictStr | None = None
model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", populate_by_name=False)

@model_validator(mode="before")
@classmethod
def preserve_legacy_mapping(cls, value):
# v1 tries dict(value), so pairs, [] and "" can become objects.
# Preserve successful conversions without changing failed-input errors.
if not isinstance(value, dict):
try:
return dict(value)
except (TypeError, ValueError):
return value
return value

def serialize_order(payload):
return OrderInput(**payload).model_dump(by_alias=True)

def preserve_legacy_error_order(fields):
# v1 reports declared-field errors first and unknown keys alphabetically.
# v2 keeps unknown keys in input order; preserve the existing HTTP contract.
known = [field for field in fields if field["code"] != "extra_forbidden"]
extra = sorted(
(field for field in fields if field["code"] == "extra_forbidden"),
key=lambda field: field["path"],
)
return known + extra

def check_target_model():
for payload, expected in (
({"order_id": "ord_123"}, {"order_id": "ord_123", "customer_note": None}),
(
{"order_id": "ord_123", "customer_note": "Leave at desk"},
{"order_id": "ord_123", "customer_note": "Leave at desk"},
),
(
{"order_id": "ord_123", "customer_note": None},
{"order_id": "ord_123", "customer_note": None},
),
):
assert serialize_order(payload) == expected
for payload, expected in (
({}, [("order_id", "missing")]),
({"order_id": 123}, [("order_id", "string_type")]),
(
{"order_id": "ord_123", "customer_note": 17},
[("customer_note", "string_type")],
),
(
{"order_id": "ord_123", "unexpected": True},
[("unexpected", "extra_forbidden")],
),
):
try:
OrderInput(**payload)
except ValidationError as error:
assert [
(item["loc"][0], item["type"]) for item in error.errors()
] == expected
else:
raise AssertionError(f"Accepted invalid order: {payload}")
print("PASS: target model validation and serialization (7 cases)")
print("Model-only checks; use --compare-stages for HTTP migration parity.")

def main():
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=ROOT / "evidence")
parser.add_argument("--compare-stages", action="store_true")
args = parser.parse_args()
if not args.compare_stages:
check_target_model()
return
args.output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
reports = []
commands = []
for stage in ("legacy", "prepared", "target"):
project = Path("support") / stage
stage_commands = [
[
"uv",
"sync",
"--project",
str(project),
"--python",
sys.executable,
"--frozen",
],
[
"uv",
"run",
"--project",
str(project),
"--python",
sys.executable,
"--frozen",
"python",
"test/run_stage.py",
stage,
str(args.output / f"{stage}.json"),
],
]
for command in stage_commands:
completed = subprocess.run(
command, cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True, text=True
)
label = f"{stage}-{len(commands)}"
(args.output / f"{label}.log").write_text(
completed.stdout + completed.stderr
)
commands.append(
{
"command": command,
"exit_code": completed.returncode,
"log": f"{label}.log",
}
)
(args.output / "commands.json").write_text(
json.dumps(commands, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n"
)
if completed.returncode:
print(completed.stdout + completed.stderr, file=sys.stderr)
raise SystemExit(completed.returncode)
print(completed.stdout, end="")
reports.append(json.loads((args.output / f"{stage}.json").read_text()))
assert all(report["python"] == platform.python_version() for report in reports)
for report in reports[1:]:
for key in (
"observations",
"public_openapi",
"direct_call",
"fixture_sha256",
"schema_fixture_sha256",
):
assert report[key] == reports[0][key], f"Parity failed: {key}"
assert reports[1]["lock_sha256"] == reports[2]["lock_sha256"]
native_schema_differs = (
reports[0]["native_model_schema"] != reports[2]["native_model_schema"]
)
assert native_schema_differs, "The example should expose native schema drift"
manifest = {
str(path.relative_to(ROOT)): digest(path)
for path in sorted(ROOT.rglob("*"))
if path.is_file()
and not path.resolve().is_relative_to(args.output.resolve())
and not any(
part in {".venv", "__pycache__", "evidence", ".ruff_cache"}
for part in path.relative_to(ROOT).parts
)
}
summary = {
"status": "pass",
"scope": "synthetic in-process FastAPI TestClient execution",
"stages": [report["stage"] for report in reports],
"http_cases_per_stage": reports[0]["http_cases"],
"native_model_schema_differs": native_schema_differs,
"public_http_and_schema_parity": True,
"commands": commands,
"source_sha256": manifest,
}
(args.output / "summary.json").write_text(
json.dumps(summary, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n"
)
print("PASS: legacy, prepared, target HTTP/schema/serialization contracts match")
print(
"Native model schemas differ; the existing public schema adapter is preserved."
)

Run the workflow in your repository

Write the brief. Name the module, direct callers, owner, approved versions, contract tests, out-of-scope code, and rollback instructions. Stop if the slice requires a wider dependency upgrade or changes public behavior.

Establish the baseline. Have Codex read AGENTS.md, the brief, official migration guidance, locks, callers, and tests. Record the starting commit and installed versions. Explain or repair failing baseline checks before claiming parity.

Prepare compatibility separately. If shared dependencies couple the module to other code, review that preparation first. Prove that the same fixtures pass against both the original and prepared baselines.

Migrate one slice. Use the starter prompt on this page. Change the module and its direct adapter; preserve unrelated modules and name any compatibility code that remains.

Run the same tests. Compare baseline and final HTTP/schema fixtures without changing expectations. Run affected integration, lint, and type checks, and save output tied to the final source and dependency state.

Review the handoff. Inspect the diff, observed evidence, unresolved differences, remaining bridge, and rollback. Create a draft PR only when repository tools and permissions support it. Leave merging, deployment, and another migration slice to the reviewer.

Record what was verified

Use an evidence record for each criterion:

Criterion: [behavior and test]
Environment: [setup reference; actual runtime and dependency versions]
Before: [commit/diff ID; command; exit code; observed result; evidence path]
After: [final commit/diff ID; command; exit code; observed result; evidence path]
Status: [pass / fail / blocked / not run]
Limits: [untested behavior, missing prerequisite, or required owner decision]

A successful import, lint check, or regenerated snapshot does not prove API parity. Record intentional differences separately, and rerun checks when the final source changes. When adapting the sample, include your application’s callers and services in the contract tests.

summary: Give participants one place to find the agenda, register, and share what they built.
prerequisites:
Before you start: Give hackathon participants a link they can use before, during, and after the event. Build a site where they can find the schedule, register a team, submit a demo, and explore what others made. Organizers can use the same project gallery to run demos and share the results afterward.

Gather the information you would normally send participants:

Source
Example
What it contributes

Event brief
A document with event date, time zone, location, and organizer contact
The event overview and help information

Agenda
A spreadsheet with start time, end time, session, and location or meeting link
The schedule

Participant guide
Team instructions, rules, judging criteria, submission deadline, and resource links
Instructions for joining and submitting

Decide what participants need to submit and when projects should appear in the gallery. For example, you might collect a title, a short description of what the team built, and a demo link. Use the event’s rules to decide whether entries appear immediately or when submissions close.

prompts.label: Starter prompt
prompts.text:
Use @Sites to build a hackathon site for [hackathon name] using the event brief and agenda below. The participants belong to our workspace.

Sources:
- Event brief and organizer contact: [attached file or document link].
- Agenda: [file or spreadsheet link and tab].
- Event date and time zone: [date and time zone].
- Team rules and submission requirements: [document link].
- Submission deadline and late-submission rule: [confirmed details].
- Project gallery visibility: [when submitted projects should appear and who can see them].
- Judging criteria and participant resources: [links or none].

First confirm which sources you can read and summarize the schedule, deadline, team rules, and required submission fields. Ask about gaps or conflicting times. Use only the supplied event details. Leave project choice to participants; don't suggest project ideas or example use cases.

Build an event overview, agenda, participant instructions, resource list, and organizer contact section. Make it easy to find the next session, team registration, and project submission. Show the event date and time zone with the schedule and exact submission deadline. Keep the deadline and help contact near the submission form. Link to original resources and explain that this is a reviewed copy of the event information.

Let participants register a team with its name and members, then return to add a project title, short description, and demo link. Distinguish saved drafts from submitted projects and explain any missing required fields. Show submitted projects in a gallery according to the supplied visibility rule. Require sign-in and enforce team membership on the server so members can edit only their own team's entry. Ask how membership should be confirmed before enabling team edits; don't use a typed name as proof of identity. Save registrations and submissions between visits.

Keep event information, team registrations, and project records separate so agenda edits preserve submissions. Validate required fields and demo links. Follow the supplied deadline rule; ask if it is missing. Don't edit source documents or send invitations.

Test with two fictional teams: register, submit, edit, reload, and try to edit the other team's entry directly. Check the deadline behavior and mobile layout. Identify and remove test records before the event. Keep the site private to our workspace and show a saved preview, test results, and unresolved questions before publishing.

prompts.label: Update the agenda without losing submissions
prompts.text: Read the revised agenda from [document link, spreadsheet tab, or attached file]. Show the differences in session times, locations, and the submission deadline before applying them. Keep team registrations, project submissions, and their access rules unchanged. Flag conflicting dates or missing time zones. After I confirm the changes, update the agenda and show a preview before publishing.

prompts.label: Add a submission countdown
prompts.text: Add a countdown to the confirmed submission deadline on [date and time] in [event time zone]. Keep the exact date, time, and time zone visible beside it. Show a clear message after the deadline instead of negative time. Follow the event's agreed late-submission rule; don't change whether submissions are accepted without asking. Test before, at, and after the deadline.

title: Build an onboarding portal
summary: Help new hires find their next task and practice the work they'll be doing.
prerequisites:
Before you start: Turn your first-week plan into a place where new hires can see what to do today, find the right resources, and pick up where they left off. Ask for a portal that brings daily tasks, helpful contacts, and an end-of-week practice task together, with progress saved for each person.

Choose a role and name something a new hire should be able to do by the end of the week. That goal helps you decide which resources and activities belong in the plan. Gather the materials your team already uses:

Source
Example
What it contributes

First-week plan
A document or spreadsheet with day, task, instructions, resource, and contact
The daily checklist

Team resources
A product overview, team directory, and role-specific templates
Links and context for each task

Practice task
Instructions, review criteria, and an approved example
A clear goal for the end of the week

Make tasks concrete enough that someone can tell when they’re done. “Learn the product” could become “Read the product overview and bring two questions to your buddy meeting.” Include an estimated time if your plan provides one, and explain which activities need another person’s help.

prompts.label: Starter prompt
prompts.text:
Use @Sites to build an onboarding portal for [role or team] from our first-week plan. The end-of-week goal is [for example, draft a customer kickoff agenda].

Sources:
- First-week plan: [attached file or document link].
- Product and team resources: [specific document or folder links].
- Practice-task instructions and example: [links].
- Contacts and their responsibilities: [supplied list].

First confirm which sources you can read. List the tasks by day with their source links, instructions, and contacts. Ask about missing or conflicting details; don't invent tasks, people, or company policies.

Build a welcome page, a day-by-day checklist, a resource list, helpful contacts, and the end-of-week practice task. For each task, show what to do, why it matters, what a completed task looks like, its resource link, and who can help. Include estimated times only where the plan provides them. Link the practice task to its instructions, approved example, and review criteria. Use the sequence in the supplied plan. Add a progress bar and a Continue where you left off section. Treat completion as a record of activities, not a score of job readiness.

Require sign-in and save each person's task completion between visits. Keep progress private to that person and enforce record access on the server. Keep shared task content separate from individual progress. Give tasks stable identities so an instruction or link update doesn't erase completion records.

Use a reviewed copy of the plan and links to original resources. Explain that source-document changes need a site update. Don't copy restricted resource contents into a page for a broader audience or write completion data back into source documents. If a source can't be read, ask for an accessible copy or link.

Test a new user, partial progress, a completed plan, and a second account. Confirm that progress survives reload, remains private, and isn't reset by an instruction edit. Flag resource links that still need a new hire's access check. Keep the site private to our workspace. Show a saved preview, test results, and open questions before publishing.

prompts.label: Refresh the plan from its source
prompts.text: Read the updated onboarding plan at [document link or attached file]. Compare it with the site's current tasks and show additions, removals, and changed instructions. Keep existing task identities and saved completion records wherever the task is the same. Ask me how to handle removed or substantially changed tasks. Update only the reviewed plan and resource links, then show a preview before publishing.

prompts.label: Put the next task first
prompts.text: Add a Continue where you left off section showing the signed-in person's first unfinished task, its day, instructions, resource link, and contact. Keep the full week available. Show a completion message when all tasks are done. Test a new user, a partially completed plan, and a completed plan, and confirm that each person's saved progress remains private.

Example

Team resources

Put the next action first

Refresh the plan from its source

title: See which campaigns bring in leads
summary: Compare spend, lead counts, and cost per lead by campaign, channel, and week.
prerequisites:
Before you start: Turn weekly campaign exports into a dashboard your team can explore during a review. Show spend, lead volume, and cost per lead together so colleagues can compare campaigns, narrow to a channel or week, and open the rows behind a result.

Choose the question the dashboard should help answer. You might want to find campaigns where spend increased without a similar increase in leads, or see whether a change came from one campaign or an entire channel. That question helps you choose useful filters and comparisons.

Export a spreadsheet for the period you want to review. Use one row per campaign per week and include a stable campaign ID if names can change.

Field
Sample value
Check before building

Week start
2026-10-05
All sources use the same week boundary and time zone

Campaign ID and name
SEARCH-01, Product demo
The ID identifies the same campaign in each source

Channel
Paid search
Channel names are consistent

Spend and currency
1000, USD
Values use one currency or remain in separate currency groups

Leads
25
Every campaign uses the same lead definition

Supply your team’s lead definition and the reporting period. If spend comes from an advertising report and leads come from a customer relationship management (CRM) report, also provide the agreed campaign mapping and attribution rule. Without these, the site can’t reliably connect the two reports.

prompts.label: Starter prompt
prompts.text:
Use @Sites to build a campaign dashboard for [team] from [attached spreadsheet or exact source link and tab].

Reporting context:
- Review question: [what the team wants to understand from this report].
- Period: [start and end dates].
- Currency: [currency].
- Week boundary and time zone: [definition].
- Lead definition and attribution rule: [team definition].
- Additional source and campaign-ID mapping, if needed: [file or none].

First inspect the source and show the columns, row count, date range, and sample rows. Expect one row per campaign per week with campaign ID or name, channel, spend, and leads. Flag duplicates, missing values, mixed currencies, and unmatched campaign IDs. Ask how to resolve ambiguous mappings; don't silently drop rows or invent data.

Show total spend, total leads, and cost per lead. Add campaign, channel, and week filters, a weekly trend chart, and a campaign comparison table. Let a reviewer inspect the source rows behind a selected campaign's totals. Make every card, chart, and table use the same filtered rows. Label currency, reporting period, source, and any excluded rows. Flag a partial reporting week when the supplied dates establish that it is incomplete.

Calculate cost per lead as total spend divided by total leads for the selected rows, never the average of row-level ratios. Show N/A for zero-lead ratios, distinguish missing values from zero, and show an empty state when no rows match. Keep different currencies separate unless I supply a conversion rule.

Start with a saved copy of the supplied data. Explain how to replace it with a new export without duplicating overlapping weeks. Don't describe it as live unless a supported connection is configured and tested. Don't edit source reports or campaign budgets, or infer revenue or lead quality from lead counts.

Check totals against the source. Use a separate, labeled sample to test that $1,000 with 25 leads plus $500 with five leads gives $1,500 spend, 30 leads, and $50 cost per lead; don't add these sample rows to the real report. Also test zero leads, missing values, duplicate rows, and combined filters. Check the mobile layout. Keep the dashboard private to our workspace and show a saved preview, validation results, and unresolved data questions before publishing.

prompts.label: Refresh from a connected spreadsheet
prompts.text: Check whether an available connection can read [spreadsheet link], tab [tab name], with columns [column names]. If supported, add a manual Refresh action using each visitor's own connection. Validate the new rows before replacing displayed results, preserve the current filters, and show the source, reporting period, and last successful refresh. Handle denied access and missing columns visibly. Keep this read-only; don't edit the sheet or change campaign budgets. If unsupported, retain the file-based update workflow.

prompts.label: Compare consecutive weeks
prompts.text: Compare the selected week with the previous calendar week for spend, leads, and cost per lead, using the same campaign and channel filters. Show absolute changes and the two date ranges. Calculate each period's cost per lead from its total spend and leads. Label missing prior-week data and undefined ratios as unavailable rather than zero. Check the results against a small sample before saving the update.

Supply your team’s lead definition and the reporting period. If spend comes from an advertising report and leads come from a customer relationship management (CRM) report, also provide the agreed campaign mapping and attribution rule. Without these, the site can’t reliably connect the two reports.

Connect your sources

Attach a CSV or spreadsheet in the build conversation. For a sheet in a connected app, ask ChatGPT which connections can read it, then provide the file link, tab name, and relevant range or column names. Complete any connection step it requests.
For example, name the “Weekly campaign results” file in Google Drive, the “Campaigns” tab, and columns A–F, if an available connection can read that sheet. Otherwise, export the tab as a CSV and attach it.

Ask ChatGPT to show the columns, reporting dates, row count, and a few sample rows before building. Identify blank values, duplicate campaign-week rows, and unmatched campaign IDs. Confirm how to handle them.

Start with a saved copy of the export. Label it with its source and reporting period. To update it, provide a fresh file in the same conversation and say whether it replaces the dataset or adds new weeks. Check for overlap before combining exports.

For data that loads when someone opens the site, ask ChatGPT to verify a supported read connection to the exact sheet or reporting source. Keep the site private to your workspace and test with a teammate’s connection. See data and connections.

A source link or uploaded export doesn’t create a live connection. For a connected version, request a manual Refresh action and a visible last-successful-refresh time. If access fails, show an error or previous results labeled with their refresh time rather than an empty report that looks like zero activity.

How to use it

Reconcile the totals with your export

Use the starter prompt, then compare unfiltered totals with the source. Check a small selection yourself before relying on the summary cards. For example, these hypothetical campaigns illustrate how the dashboard should combine results:

Sample campaign
Spend
Leads
Cost per lead

Product demo: Search
$1,000
25
$40

Product demo: Social
$500
5
$100

Combined
$1,500
30
$50

Combined cost per lead is $1,500 divided by 30 leads, or $50. Averaging $40 and $100 would incorrectly give $70 because the campaigns generated different numbers of leads. Ask ChatGPT to show how it calculates the total, then check it against your source rows.

Test a zero-lead row, a missing value, and a filter with no matching rows. The cards, chart, and table should all use the same selection and distinguish missing data from zero.

Compare volume, cost, and weekly changes

Choose the same reporting period for the campaigns you want to compare. Look at lead counts alongside cost per lead: a campaign can have a low unit cost while contributing only a small share of total leads. Then filter to a channel and inspect the weekly trend to find where a change began.

Use the campaign table to identify what needs a closer look. If spend rose but leads stayed flat, check the source report and campaign changes for that period. If one week looks unusually low, first check whether the week is complete and all rows were included. Lead counts alone don’t establish lead quality, revenue, or what caused a change.

Bring current data to the weekly review

Review the audience and publish the dashboard for your team. Before each meeting, replace the export or refresh the connected source, then verify the reporting period, totals, and any excluded rows. In the meeting, filter to a result someone has a question about and trace it back to the source. Leave with a specific follow-up, such as checking a campaign’s lead definition or reviewing a recent creative change. Keep budget changes outside the dashboard’s reporting workflow.

Take it further

Refresh from a connected spreadsheet

Replace repeated file uploads with a supported read connection that shows when the dashboard last refreshed successfully.

Check whether an available connection can read [spreadsheet link], tab [tab name], with columns [column names]. If supported, add a manual Refresh action using each visitor's own connection. Validate the new rows before replacing displayed results, preserve the current filters, and show the source, reporting period, and last successful refresh. Handle denied access and missing columns visibly. Keep this read-only; don't edit the sheet or change campaign budgets. If unsupported, retain the file-based update workflow. 

Compare consecutive weeks

Show what changed from the previous calendar week, using consistent filters and totals for both periods.

Compare the selected week with the previous calendar week for spend, leads, and cost per lead, using the same campaign and channel filters. Show absolute changes and the two date ranges. Calculate each period's cost per lead from its total spend and leads. Label missing prior-week data and undefined ratios as unavailable rather than zero. Check the results against a small sample before saving the update.

title: Turn an issue into a tested pull request
summary: Hand off a small feature with acceptance criteria and review the evidence.

prompts.label: Starter prompt
prompts.text:
Implement [issue ID and title] in [repository] at [base branch and commit],
using the prepared cloud environment I selected for this task.

Input packet: [paste or attach the issue, acceptance criteria, relevant
files, public success/error schemas, authorization and pagination contract,
test fixtures, and approved validation commands].
Repository instructions: [AGENTS.md and any relevant nested instructions].
Scope: [files or component boundaries].
Out of scope: [explicit exclusions].
Required checks: [focused tests, relevant regression tests, type check,
lint, and any required CI checks].
Output: [create a draft PR in this repository if the available integration
supports it and I authorize it here / return a diff and draft PR description].

First read the instructions and relevant code. Confirm the starting commit
and run the existing baseline checks using the execution tools available
in this environment. Record any new test files as still to be created.
If the baseline fails, access is missing, or a
required check cannot run, report the exact blocker before implementing.

State a short plan, then implement the smallest change that meets the
acceptance criteria. Follow existing auth, error, pagination, and testing
patterns. Add tests that distinguish the required behavior from the old
behavior. For this pagination example, require tied timestamps across a
page boundary, bounded traversal and replay on fixed fixtures, partial and
exact-full final pages, authorization before cursor validation, invalid
cursor cases, and success/error schema checks. Update the affected API
documentation to match the implemented public response exactly.

After implementation, run the required checks again. For every acceptance
criterion, point to the test or other evidence that verifies it. Record
commands, results, the tested commit or working-tree state, and any checks
that were not run. Separate pre-existing failures from new failures.
Never describe an unrun check as passing.

Deliver the diff or authorized draft PR, a concise change summary, the
acceptance-criteria evidence table, remaining risks, and reviewer actions.
Do not merge, deploy, use production data, change permissions, add new
dependencies, or expand the agreed scope. Stop for a decision if the
contract conflicts with the repository or the work needs a schema change.
